item.semiconductor-lab.electromagnet.not: Iron wound with copper wire that is a magnet only while current flows.
Crafting: 1 iron ingot (core) + 8 copper wire (wire drawing [1-58]) → 1. A part for the magnet that sorts ions by mass in ion implantation [9-28] and more.
Current makes a magnetic field around it. Many turns add up the field and the iron core strengthens it further. Switch off the current and it is plain iron again.

In 1820 Ørsted found that a current deflects a compass needle. In 1825 Sturgeon wound copper wire on iron to make an electromagnet, and in the 1830s Henry wound many turns of insulated wire to lift heavy loads.
item.semiconductor-lab.electromagnet.pla: Approximation: wire insulation (once silk) is not modelled. It is a part item and does not act as a block.
item.semiconductor-lab.microcomputer.not: A tiny computer built from your own CPU and ROM chips. Right-click to run its program.
Chips that passed the 4-bit CPU (cpu4) and ROM (rom_program) challenges, a quartz resonator (clock) and a Nixie tube, on the assembly bench.
Intel MCS-4 (1971): the 4004 CPU, 4001 ROM, 4002 RAM and 4003 ran Busicom's 141-PF calculator. Change the program and it does another job: a general-purpose part.
Four instructions (LOAD, ADD, OUT, JUMP, one-hot), an 8-word ROM (the 4001 had 256). It runs on the reference CPU; your chips were proven by the challenges.
